title: Canon law
hook: the Church's law ends by saying its highest rule is the salvation of souls

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy See: the pope's office, a seat rather than a city, protected by a tiny state. Your line was the see of Peter.

Skip to the last page of a rulebook and you'll usually find an index, a clause about definitions, or nothing at all. The Catholic Church's book of law is thick, numbered from start to finish, full of rules about marriages, parishes, property and courts. A reader who skips to the end finds a short canon about moving a parish priest from one parish to another. And in its very last words, the whole book says what all the other rules are for.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A RULEBOOK.` → `MARRIAGES, PARISHES, PROPERTY, COURTS.` → `THE LAST WORDS SAY WHAT IT'S FOR.`

segments.voice: Canon law is the Church's own law, the rules by which the Catholic Church orders its life: who may be ordained, how a parish is set up, how a marriage case is heard. This week has leaned on it again and again, for secular institutes, the parish, the diocese and the Holy See. The Latin Church has its Code of Canon Law; the Eastern Catholic Churches have their own code. What canon law is not: the faith itself, or a list of everything holy. It's more like the plumbing and wiring of a house: unglamorous, mostly unnoticed, and badly missed when it fails. Now, that last canon. It deals with a hard moment: a bishop needs to transfer a pastor who doesn't want to go. The canon tells the bishop to act with fairness, what canonists call canonical equity, and to keep before his eyes the salvation of souls, which, it says, must always be the supreme law in the Church. In Latin, the key words are salus animarum. So the book ends not with a penalty but with a purpose, and every rule in it is meant to be read in that light. Jesus describes himself in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." Canon law is the Church's attempt to organize shepherding, and its final line reminds every bishop, priest and judge that the sheep are the point.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S OWN LAW.` · `PLUMBING AND WIRING, NOT THE HOUSE.` · `THE LAST CANON: THE SALVATION OF SOULS.` · `THE SHEEP ARE THE POINT.` · then, large: `THE SUPREME LAW IN THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Let the last canon's idea come slowly: fairness, and before your eyes, the salvation of souls, the supreme law. Then think of one rule you keep at home or at work, and ask what it's for, and whether it still serves the people it was made for. If you pray, bring that rule and the people it touches to God; if you don't, sit with the question.
Canon law. The Church's own law, whose final canon names the salvation of souls as its supreme law. Today's word.
Your line: for souls. Every rule in the book is there to serve them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic dioceses have canon lawyers and church courts, called tribunals, that apply canon law, including in marriage cases. Priests and bishops study it as part of their training.
